title: I Started Writing Online Before My 9-to-5. 6 Months Later, It Completely Changed My Life
author: Eve Arnold
summary: Arnold tells the origin story of her writing career as an argument about self-trust rather than an argument about publishing. She opens in 2020, stuck in a job she disliked and caught in a loop of consuming other people's success stories, which made the gap between her life and theirs feel wider rather than smaller. The turn comes not from a plan but from exhaustion with her own excuses, a moment in the car where she gave herself the choice of acting or of shutting up about it. What she found on the other side of starting was that the thing she had built up in her head was neither big nor scary, a discovery she treats as the real lesson rather than the traffic that followed. Six months in, one hurried piece went viral, and she is careful to say the value was not the money or the followers but the signal it sent to her brain, which she names as self-belief. The essay ends on a quieter claim about outcome: the writing changed what she wanted, trading the high-flying executive ambition for a part-time business and a simple life in the country, and it made her someone who does what she says she will.
points: The piece locates the turning point in boredom with her own excuses rather than in a strategy, a plan, or a new opportunity.
Arnold argues that the value of the viral post was informational rather than financial, because it told her she had been spending her effort on the wrong things rather than being broken.
She frames starting as a way of testing a fear, finding that the imagined difficulty of publishing was far larger than the actual act.
The reported outcome is a revision of ambition, moving from climbing a corporate ladder toward a quiet life with a part-time business alongside the job.
Her final measure of success is character rather than income: becoming a person who follows through on what she says she will do.
quotes: I was stuck in a job I hated, had no idea what I wanted to do with my life, and I would just spend hours watching videos on repeat of people making $10k/month, wondering how I’d gotten everything so wrong.
It was the millionth day in a row that I was having the same conversation with myself. Something snapped. I was bored of my own excuses.
So I did. I just started. I found this site called Medium, and I thought I’d give writing a shot. I had nothing to lose and a lot to say.
But what it did teach me was this thing I’d been making out in my head, this big scary thing, wasn’t big or scary at all.
Not because of the money or the followers or anything like that, but because of the signal it sent to my brain. Because it gave me something you can’t put a price on — self-belief.
For the longest time, I’d tried and failed at a bunch of businesses. You name it, I’d tried it, so I was starting to think it was me that was broken.

I’ve gone from thinking I wanted to be a high-flying executive to choosing a quiet, simple life in the country. I’ve gone from climbing the ladder to working 9-to-5 and running a part-time business on the internet.
And here’s the biggie, and the most important outcome by far — it’s turned me into a person I like. I don’t wake up each day now wishing I was doing more or wanting to be more fulfilled.
